**Surah Ta-Ha**, upon him be the best of prayers and the most complete of peace (ﷺ).

Its purpose is to inform that those who are called (to faith) are given respite, shown forbearance, and treated gently until they become the most numerous of nations, which increases the honour of their caller (ﷺ). This noble purpose is indicated by the surah's name through symbolism and allusion, so that people of insight and discernment may understand it. This is shown by the **disjoined letters** (*al-huruf al-muqatta'ah*, the isolated letters that open some surahs) at its beginning. When the end of **Surah Maryam** caused fear that his community would be destroyed before the command that Allah had given him became manifest and his call became well known, because few of them had believed in him, Allah began with the letter **ṭā'** (ط). Its point of articulation is the tip of the tongue and the roots of the two upper front teeth, indicating the strength of his affair, its spread, its elevation, and the great number of his followers. This articulation point produces more letters than the others, is the most active in movement, and has the widest reach. Its attributes of *jahr* (voicing), *iṭbāq* (pressing the tongue against the palate), *istiʿlā'* (elevation), and *qalqalah* (the echoing vibration of certain letters) indicate that what was hidden will become openly declared, and what was gentle will become emphatic. This is because it is among the letters of emphasis (*tafkhim*). It also indicates that his affair will rise, his mention will spread until it covers all existence, and it will shake the rest of the nations. However, this will happen in the manner indicated by the letter **hā'** (ه). Its point of articulation is the furthest part of the throat, far from the tip of the tongue, which indicates a long duration and a great deal of time. Its attributes of *hams* (breathiness), *rakhāwah* (softness), *infitāḥ* (openness), *istifāl* (lowering), and concealment, together with a whisper and great weakness, great calm, and great hiddenness, indicate enduring great hardships, along with a kind of grandeur and fame. Although this fame is slight, it overcomes all this weakness, even though the weakness is strong and severe. The *imālah* reading of the hā' (inclining the vowel) indicates the severity of the weakness. The *tafkhim* reading, which is the reading of most of the reciters (*qurrā'*), indicates the grandeur of the rank and the strength of the affair, through the openness that it contains. Although it is seen that this is not so in the verse "Indeed, the king of the Banu al-Asfar fears him" (the Byzantine emperor). And even though the meaning of the two letters is "O man," they indicate his strength, the loftiness of his rank, the grandeur of his mention, the spread of his followers, and the generality of his affair. And if they indicate the treading of the earth, this points to the strength of his establishment, the greatness of his power, and the breadth of his renown, until all of it becomes a dominion for him and his followers, and a dominion for his commanders and partisans. And Allah knows best.

Ibn al-Furat mentioned in his history that the migration to Abyssinia occurred in the eighth year after the mission. Apparently, according to what comes later regarding the conversion of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), the revelation of this surah, or its beginning, occurred near the time of the migration to Abyssinia. Thus Allah signalled to him (ﷺ), in a manner sweeter in intimate conversation with the beloved than direct address, through the numerical value of the name of the letter ṭā' (9), that the extreme weakness of the disbelievers would occur in the ninth year after its revelation, which was the Battle of Badr al-Mawʿid in the fourth year of the Hijrah. Through the numerical value of its name (ṭāhā, which gives the total of 14), He indicated that the first conquest would occur in the eleventh year after its revelation, which was the 'Umrah of al-Hudaybiyah in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the sixth year of the Hijrah, at the revelation of **Surah al-Fath**. He signalled through the numerical value of the letter hā' (5) that the beginning of victory through the Hijrah would occur in the fifth year after its revelation. Through the numerical value of its name (ṭāhā, 14), He indicated that his victory in actuality would occur in the seventh year after its revelation, which was the Battle of Badr al-Kubra in the second year of the Hijrah. Through the numerical value of the two letters of its name, not the numerical value of its two names, He indicated that in the thirteenth year after its revelation there would be the conquest of the Greatest, through prevailing over Makkah the Honoured, which was a close cause for prevailing over all the earth. This occurred at the end of it, in Ramadan of the eighth year of the Hijrah. Its completion was the conquest of al-Ta'if through the sending of their delegation, their conversion to Islam, and the destruction of their idol in the ninth year, which was the fourteenth year. Through the numerical value of its two names, He indicated that the spread of Islam over most of the earth would occur in the eighteenth year after its revelation, which was in the caliphate of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) in the thirteenth year of the Hijrah. And Allah knows best.

"**Bismi**" (in the name of) the All-Encompassing in forbearance, the perfect in power. "**Allāhi**" (of Allah), the Greatest King. "**al-Raḥmāni**" (the Most Merciful), the One through whose original blessing all His creation is equal. "**al-Raḥīmi**" (the Most Compassionate), the One who completed His blessing upon the people of His success and His kindness.

﴿Ta-Ha﴾: that is, a complete deliverance from everything one fears, a great prominence, and a good fragrance spreading in every region up to the furthest extent of the land, which is the ninth, from the One who has complete encompassment of every unseen thing, and to whom the whole affair returns. Likewise, all His names are gathered in a hidden matter, He who made honour belong to those who are guided and guidance belong to the God-fearing.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):**

This surah and the one before it are among the earliest Meccan surahs. Ibn Hisham, in *Tahdhib al-Sirah*, said: Ibn Ishaq said: Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Zuhri narrated to me, from Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham al-Makhzumi, from Umm Salamah bint Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: She said: "When we settled in the land of Abyssinia, we were given the best of neighbours by the Negus (al-Najashi). We were secure in our religion, we worshipped Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, and we were not harmed, nor did we hear anything we disliked. When this reached Quraysh, they conspired among themselves," and he mentioned their sending to him with gifts so that he would return them, and that his patriarchs (*batariqah*) spoke to him about it, and that he refused until he had heard their words, and that he summoned them. Their matter was settled on speaking the truth, whatever the consequence. So they entered, and the Negus had summoned his bishops (*asaqifah*), who spread their scriptures (*masahif*) around him. He said to them: "What is this religion for which you have separated from your people, and which you have not entered into any of these faiths (*milal*)?"

She said: "The one who spoke to him was Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: 'O King! We were a people of ignorance (*jahiliyyah*). We worshipped idols, we ate carrion, we committed abominations, we severed the ties of kinship, we treated neighbours badly, and the strong among us devoured the weak. We remained in this state until Allah sent to us a Messenger from among us, whose lineage, truthfulness, trustworthiness and chastity we knew. He called us to Allah, that we should affirm His oneness and worship Him, and cast off what we and our fathers used to worship besides Him of stones and idols. He commanded us to speak the truth, to fulfil trusts, to maintain ties of kinship, to be good to neighbours, to refrain from what is forbidden and from bloodshed. He forbade us from abominations, false speech, consuming the property of orphans, and slandering chaste women. He commanded us to worship Allah alone and not associate anything with Him, and commanded us to pray, to give zakat and to fast.'" She said: "He enumerated for him the matters of Islam. So we believed him and affirmed him, but our people attacked us, tortured us and tried to turn us away from our religion, so that they might return us to the worship of idols. When they overpowered and oppressed us, we left for your land, choosing you over others, and we hoped that we would not be wronged in your presence, O King!"

The Negus said to him: "Do you have with you any of what he brought from Allah?" Ja'far said: "Yes!" The Negus said to him: "Then recite it to me." So he recited to him the opening of Surah Maryam: ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾. The Negus wept, by Allah, until his beard was drenched, and his bishops wept until their scriptures were drenched, when they heard what he recited to them. Then the Negus said: "Indeed, this and what Moses brought come from the same niche (*mishkah*)." Then he mentioned his granting them protection, and the return of the gifts of Quraysh and their envoys, disappointed.

Ibn Hisham said: Ibn Ishaq said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Abd Allah ibn Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah narrated to me, from Abd al-Aziz ibn Abd Allah ibn Amir ibn Rabi'ah, from his mother Umm Abd Allah bint Abi Hathmah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "By Allah! We were preparing to journey to the land of Abyssinia, while Amir, may Allah be pleased with him, had gone off on some of our errands. Then Umar ibn al-Khattab came and stood over me, while he was still upon his polytheism. We used to suffer affliction from him, harm to us and severity towards us. He said: 'Is it departure, O Umm Abd Allah?' I said: 'Yes! By Allah, we shall go out into the earth of Allah. You have harmed us and oppressed us, until Allah makes a way out for us.' He said: 'May Allah accompany you.' I saw in him a tenderness I had not seen before. Then he left, and it seemed that our departure had grieved him. When Amir, may Allah be pleased with him, came back with his errand, I said to him: 'O Abu Abd Allah! If only you had seen Umar just now, with his tenderness and his sorrow over us!' He said: 'Do you hope he will embrace Islam?' I said: 'Yes!' He said: 'The one you saw will not embrace Islam until the donkey of al-Khattab embraces it,' out of despair of him, because of the harshness and hardness of his character towards Islam."

Ibn Ishaq said: "Umar's conversion, as it reached me, was that his sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab, who was married to Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, may Allah be pleased with them both, had embraced Islam, and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd had also embraced Islam, and they were concealing their Islam from Umar. Nu'aym ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Nahham, a man of his people from the clan of Bani Adi ibn Ka'b, had also embraced Islam, may Allah be pleased with him, and he too concealed his Islam out of fear of his people. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, may Allah be pleased with him, used to visit Fatimah bint al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with her, to recite the Qur'an to her. One day Umar went out with his sword slung on him, intending the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a group of his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, who had told him that they had gathered in a house near al-Safa, about forty men and women, and with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was his uncle Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah al-Siddiq, and Ali ibn Abi Talib, with men of the Muslims, may Allah be pleased with them all, from among those who had remained with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Mecca and had not gone out with those who went to the land of Abyssinia. Nu'aym ibn Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, met him and said: 'Where are you going, O Umar?' He said: 'I am going to Muhammad, this apostate (*sabi'*) who has divided the affair of Quraysh, made foolish their minds, reviled their religion and cursed their gods. I will kill him.' Nu'aym, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: 'By Allah! Your own soul has deluded you, O Umar! Do you think the sons of Abd Manaf will let you walk the earth after you have killed Muhammad? Will you not return to your household and set their affairs right?' He said: 'And which household of mine?' He said: 'Your brother-in-law and cousin Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn Amr, and your sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab. By Allah, they have both embraced Islam and followed Muhammad in his religion, so go to them.'"

Umar then returned intending his sister and brother-in-law, and with them was Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, may Allah be pleased with him and with them, and he had with him a sheet (*sahifah*) on which was Ta-Ha, which he was reciting to them. When they heard Umar's sound, Khabbab hid himself in an inner chamber (*makhda'*) of theirs or in some part of the house, and Fatimah bint al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with her, took the sheet and put it under her thigh. Umar, as he drew near the house, had heard Khabbab's recitation to them. When he entered he said: "What is this murmur (*hay'amah*) I heard?" They said to him: "You heard nothing." He said: "Yes! By Allah, I have been told that you have both followed Muhammad in his religion!" And he laid hands on his brother-in-law Sa'id ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him. His sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab rose to him to restrain him from her husband, and he struck her and split her head open. When he had done that, his sister and brother-in-law, may Allah be pleased with them both, said to him: "Yes! We have embraced Islam and believed in Allah and His Messenger, so do what you wish!"

When Umar saw the blood on his sister, he regretted what he had done (*fa-ir'awa*, he relented) and said to his sister: "Give me this sheet which I heard you reading just now. Let me see what this is that Muhammad has brought." Umar was a writer. When he said that, his sister said to him: "We fear for it on your account." He said: "Do not fear." And he swore to her by his gods that he would return it to her once he had read it. When he said that, she hoped he would embrace Islam, and she said to him: "O my brother! You are unclean in your polytheism, and none may touch it but the pure." So Umar stood up and washed, and she gave him the sheet in which was Ta-Ha, and he read it. When he had read a portion of it he said: "How excellent and how noble is this speech!" When Khabbab heard that, he came out to him and said: "O Umar! By Allah, I hope that Allah has singled you out with the supplication of His Prophet (ﷺ), for I heard him yesterday say: 'O Allah! Strengthen Islam with Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham (Abu Jahl) or with Umar ibn al-Khattab. So, by Allah, fear Allah, O Umar!'" Umar said to him at that point: "Then direct me, O Khabbab, to Muhammad, so that I may go to him and embrace Islam." Khabbab said to him: "He is in a house near al-Safa, with a group of his Companions in it." So Umar took his sword, slung it on himself, and made straight for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions, and struck the door upon them. When they heard his voice, a man from among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up and looked through a crack in the door, and saw him with the sword slung on him. He returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in alarm and said: "O Messenger of Allah! This is Umar ibn al-Khattab with his sword slung on him!" Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Admit him. If he has come seeking good, we shall give it to him, and if he has come seeking evil, we shall kill him with his own sword." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Admit him." The man admitted him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose to him and met him in the room (*hujrah*), seized him by his waistband or by the gathering of his cloak, and pulled him with a violent pull, and said: "What has brought you, O son of al-Khattab? By Allah, I do not think you will stop until Allah sends down upon you a calamity (*qari'ah*)!" Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have come to you to believe in Allah and His Messenger and in what has come from Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then uttered the takbir (*Allahu akbar*) in a loud exclamation, so that the people of the house among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew that Umar had embraced Islam. The Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) dispersed from their places, having felt strengthened in themselves when Umar ibn al-Khattab embraced Islam, along with the Islam of Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with them both, and they knew that the two of them would protect the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and that they would gain redress (*yantasifun*) through them against their enemies."

This is the narration of the transmitters from the people of Medina concerning Umar's conversion, may Allah be pleased with him, when he embraced Islam. Umar's conversion came three days after Hamzah's conversion, may Allah be pleased with them both, as this is established in the margin of the commentary on *Sharh al-Aqa'id*, citing *Fawa'id Tamam* by al-Razi, and in *Safwat al-Safwah* by Ibn al-Jawzi.

Ibn Hisham said: Ibn Ishaq said: Nafi', the freedman of Abd Allah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, narrated to me, saying: "When Umar embraced Islam, he said: 'Which of Quraysh is the best at carrying tales (*anqal lil-hadith*)?'" It was said to him: "Jamil ibn Ma'mar al-Jumahi." So he set out to him. Abd Allah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I set out following his tracks and watching what he did, while I was a boy who understood everything I saw, until he came to him and said: 'Do you know, O Jamil, that I have embraced Islam and entered the religion of Muhammad?'" He said: "By Allah, he did not even answer him, but rose trailing his cloak." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, followed him, and I followed my father, until he stood at the door of the mosque and cried out at the top of his voice: "O assembly of Quraysh!" They were in their gathering-places around the Ka'bah. "Beware! Ibn al-Khattab has apostatized (*saba'*)!" Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said from behind him: "He lied! But I have embraced Islam, and I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger." They rushed at him, and he did not cease fighting them and they fighting him, until the sun stood over their heads. He said: "He sat down, exhausted (*tala'a*), and they stood over his head, while he said: 'Do whatever you wish! By Allah, were we three hundred men, we would have left the city to you, or you would have left it to us.'" While he was in that state, there came a shaykh of Quraysh wearing a striped cloak (*hibarah*) and an embroidered shirt, until he stood over them and said: "What is the matter with you?" They said: "Umar has apostatized (*sabi'a*)." He said: "Stop! A man has chosen for himself a course. What do you want? Do you think the Bani Adi ibn Ka'b will surrender to you their companion? Such is the man!" He said: "By Allah, it was as though they were a garment from which he had been stripped."

In *al-Rawd al-Unuf* by the Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli, it is related that Yunus narrated from Ibn Ishaq that Umar, when he embraced Islam, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of favour, to whom are owed blessings upon us which have no alteration.

We had begun, and we denied, and He said to us, the true speech of a Prophet with whom is the news.

I had wronged the daughter of al-Khattab, then my Lord guided me on an evening when they said, "Umar has turned away."

And I have repented of what was a slip, in wronging her, when the surahs are recited in her presence.

When she called upon her Lord, Lord of the Throne, striving, while the tears from her eye were hastening and flowing.

I was certain that the One she calls upon is her Creator, and a pearl-like tear nearly outran me.

So I said: "I bear witness that Allah is our Creator, and that Ahmad is today renowned among us."

A Prophet of truth who came with the truth from one trusted, faithful in trust, in whose core there is no weakness.

Having established this, it becomes clear that the purpose of the surah, as mentioned earlier, is to honor this noble Prophet (ﷺ) by informing him of the gentleness toward his community and of their hearts turning towards him, until they fill the earth in multitude; just as He sent down tranquility upon them while they were in the utmost weakness and scarcity, and protected them from those who sought to kill them; and He softened the heart of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) after the harshness that had been in him, and made him a minister. Then He protected him (ﷺ) from his enemy, and assured him that they would not be utterly destroyed by a punishment, and that their prophet would die before them, unlike what befell the destroyed peoples of Noah and Hud (peace be upon them both) and those after them. This is indicated by the opening of this surah with the negation of misery, and the closing of that one with the granting of affection, among other things. The motive for this assurance is that when He, glory be to Him, concluded that surah with the destruction of generations and the annihilation of nations after warning the stubborn people, and had not concluded any of the preceding surahs with the like of that, it [might] have suggested that their term had ended, their ruin had come, and their destruction had arrived, and that none of them would believe, because of the obstinacy they were in, except those who had already believed. Thus there resulted in him (ﷺ) such grief and sorrow as none knows the extent of except Allah, because the matter was still in its beginning, and only a very small band of them had embraced Islam. So Allah, glory be to Him, calmed his dread with His saying:

﴿We did not send down﴾ by Our greatness ﴿upon you﴾, meaning while you are the most knowledgeable of creation, ﴿the Qur'an﴾, meaning the greatest of books, gathering every good and repelling every harm, which We made easy by your tongue, ﴿that you should suffer﴾, meaning through the weariness of your heart, since you are among the fewest of messengers in followers, after the uprooting of your people and their wretchedness through your warning.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 3:

﴿Except﴾, that is, "but rather, We sent it down" (p-267) ﴿as a reminder﴾, that is, a great reminder, ﴿for those who fear﴾, from among those whom he indicated at the end of the preceding surah with the good news of them. This is a hint that among them there will be a number of the God-fearing, whose abundance is fitting for the inimitability (i'jaz) of this Qur'an and its permanence, and for the comprehensive collection that is referred to by the expression "the Qur'an," which includes all the rulings in the earlier Scriptures, both principles and derivative rulings, along with exhortations and subtleties, knowledge and etiquette, the reports of the former and latter peoples, the welfare of both abodes, and additions to them by what God willed. This is because the abundance of the community is in proportion to the greatness of the Book. The expression of "but rather" by an allusion indicates that it is possible that it belongs to the category of:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords
are, by them, notched from the clashing of battalions."

The verbal noun used in place of the verb in His saying ﴿a revelation (tanzilan)﴾ indicates that He proceeds gently with them, out of kindness toward them, and does not send down this Qur'an except gradually: to remove their doubts, to open their hearts, to calm their souls, and to extend the period of blessing among them through the repeated descent of the noble angels to them. Likewise, He did not destroy them for their disobediences, being content with the clear evidence of what is in the earlier scriptures, but sent a Messenger to them so that they would not say: "Our Lord, if only" (as His wisdom required and His word was fulfilled by it). Since their return to the religion, given the harshness, arrogance and obstinacy that is observed in them, for which God named them a "quarrelsome people" (qawman ludda), was extremely remote, He, glory be to Him, began to remind of His power, as an indication that hearts are in His hand: He turns them however He wills, just as He fashioned them however He willed, and that His way is gentleness and patience. So He said, shifting from the first person plural to the third person, to show what the "we" implied of majesty (p-268) [presenting what the situation required to be presented: the dwelling of those addressed, who are cared for in their admonition and in guiding those for whom it was intended]: ﴿Of Him who created the earth﴾, the lowly one.

When He put the earth first, to announce His care for its surface by treating its inhabitants gently, so that He would fill it with faith from among them, realizing the aim of the surah by honoring [the one to whom it was sent down], He followed it with the place of descent by way of ascent, from the House of Honor (bayt al-'izza) to what He stored in the treasury of the Throne (al-'arsh). So He said: ﴿and the high heavens﴾, in six days, though had He willed, they would have been in a moment.

Since the Almighty may not be a king, He stated, to indicate His sovereignty and praising Him with certainty, a predicate for an omitted subject: ﴿The Most Merciful﴾, beginning with the attribute that bestows general blessings upon the obedient and the disobedient alike. [Then he mentioned a second predicate indicating the comprehensiveness of mercy, saying:] ﴿Established Himself upon the Throne﴾, which encompasses all of that, ﴿istawā﴾, meaning He began to manage all of that alone. He addressed the servants in terms they would understand from their saying, "So-and-so istawā," meaning he sat upright upon the throne of kingship, and so he alone managed it, even if there is no throne there and no sitting upon it at all. This is the spirit of this expression, just as the spirit of his saying, upon him be blessings and peace, narrated by Muslim from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The hearts are between two of the fingers of Allah; He turns them however He wills," is that He, glorified and exalted, is greatly capable of that, and it is easy for Him, light, just as it is light for one in whose case this is the situation. The intended meaning is not that there is a finger there at all. Ḥujjat al-Islām al-Ghazālī (d. 505 AH) drew attention to this, and from it al-Zamakhsharī (d. 538 AH) derived that "So-and-so's hand is outstretched" is a metaphor (kināyah) for generosity, even if there is no hand there and no outstretching at all.

Since a king may not necessarily own what he rules, He said, placing the more noble first as is customary: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾, that is, all of it, whether rational or otherwise, ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾, all of it, ﴿and whatever is between them﴾, that is, between the heavens and the earth, ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾, which is the moist earth, whether we say that it is the lowest part of the world, so that beneath it is pure non-existence, or not. In that case there would be beneath it light, or a fish, or other things.

Since a king cannot govern in the fullest sense of governing except through comprehensive knowledge, and since a human king may not know the conditions of the farthest reaches of his realm as he knows those of the nearest, especially if it is vast, and for this reason some of his affairs fall into disorder, He (glory be to Him) informed that He is the opposite of that. So He said, urging vigilance over Him and sincerity toward Him: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret, and what is yet more hidden.﴾ That is, with this Qur'an, for giving glad tidings and warning, or for other purposes, or with other than it. For He knows it, and has no need of loudness, so let there be no affectation of that in what you were not commanded to say aloud for a purpose other than making it heard. ﴿Indeed He knows the secret﴾, which is what two people confide to one another in a low voice. ﴿And what is yet more hidden﴾ than that, which is what is in the hearts of things that thoughts have imagined but that has not come forth into the outside world (p-270), and other than that of the unseen which no one but Him, exalted is He, knows in any way whatsoever, and among it is what will come to be in the hearts.

[ - Since one who has these attributes is of complete knowledge and power ] it might be thought that He has a rival. He negated that by His saying, informing that this supposition is absolutely false, with no basis for doubt, and that what preceded necessarily produces this conclusion: ﴿Allah﴾, opening with the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam), which comprises the attributes of majesty and others, ﴿there is no god but He﴾. Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, that is, to Him alone, the attributes of perfection, which cannot admit, nor is it conceivable that they admit, any deficiency whatsoever. Rather, He is characterized by them always, with a true characterization that cannot be separated from Him, unlike others, who may be characterized by some excellences at some times and then be unable to attain them at another time or with respect to another period.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 9:

When He followed this with the story of Moses (peace be upon him), beginning with an interrogative (istifham) joined to a conjunctive waw (waw al-'atf), this indicates that the meaning is: "Do you know of any namesake for Him", that is, one who is characterised by His attributes, or by some of them, so that he has an action like His action through that attribute. Since the answer is definitively "No", it is established that none is characterised by any of His attributes. So He conjoined the story of Moses (peace be upon him) to this implied clause. The implied sense is: "Have you known, from what We have reminded you of in these verses, that We intend what is easy for Us, by the complete power and all-encompassing knowledge We possess, to make you happy in both abodes by multiplying your reward and magnifying your affair, by multiplying (p-271) your followers." He conjoined to it the story as a tangible witness to what He has of the attributes by which others are negated, of the Most Beautiful Names, and especially what is mentioned here of being characterised by perfect power and singularity in greatness. And that He exalts this chosen one by sending down this Remembrance upon him and conveying it from Him to him: victory over kings and all opponents, establishment in the regions of the lands, abundance of followers, strengthening of helpers, ministers and partisans, and other things, by the measure of the difference between the beginnings of their two affairs. For the beginning of Moses' affair (peace be upon him) was that he came to the fire to bring a brand for his family, or to find guidance by it. So by that He granted him guidance in both abodes and victory over enemies, as He will recount here what He granted. And this noble Prophet's beginning was that he went to the Cave of Hira', worshipping there for many nights, and provisioning himself for that, drawn by the Truth towards him before prophethood with a supply, as training for him and strengthening of his heart. Then prophethood came to him while he was traversing its arena, and he was ascending to its summit by his resolve, rather flying. And Moses (peace be upon him), when prophethood came to him, saw the sign of the staff and the hand. Muhammad (ﷺ), before prophethood, would not pass by a stone or a tree without it greeting him, as Ibn Ishaq related in the Sirah (Ibn Ishaq's Life of the Prophet). Muslim and others narrated from Jabir ibn Samurah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I know a stone that used to greet me before I was sent (as a prophet)." Then He said, affirming and alerting, indicating that He mentions to him from it what suffices for his consolation and the strengthening of his heart, and for the rebuke of the Jews who hesitated regarding his affair (ﷺ), and who deceived the Quraysh when they undertook to cross the distance of separation to them, and were pleased with their statement to them against them. So the benefit of the interrogation is that he should empty his noble ear for listening and his heart for great comprehension: ﴿And has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ That is, O best of creation! ﴿The story of Moses﴾, urging emulation of Moses (peace be upon him) in bearing the burdens of prophethood, undertaking the mission and enduring patiently the stations of hardship; and explaining, by mentioning what is in this surah, the context of the story of what was summarised of it in [Surat Maryam]; and affirming, by what He arranged in its forms of expression, what was earlier stated to be the purpose of the surah, that He makes him happy and does not make him wretched, and grants him honour over all who hate him, by honouring him over the people of his land after they expelled him, just as Moses (peace be upon him) was honoured over those who left their lands fearful and watchful. This encourages emigration (hijrah) a third time, after encouraging it first by the story of the People of [the Cave], and second by the story of [his forefather] Abraham (peace be upon him). And that He will exalt his people over all the people of the earth, and will rescue them through him after their weakness from every hardship, enrich their poverty, and make them kings of the earth, humbling tyrants through them, and destroying whoever among them He knew to be wretched, just as He did with the people of Moses. He also alluded, by the rescue of Moses (peace be upon him) at the hand of his enemy, and the casting of love upon him, and the guidance of the magicians while Pharaoh and his people were not guided, and the worship of the calf by the Children of Israel after they had seen the signs, blessings and punishments, then their return from it, to His great power over the turning of hearts, for the one who was consuming himself in grief over their disbelief in this report; and likewise what is in the story of Adam (peace be upon him) of His saying ﴿So he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], and His saying ﴿Then his Lord chose him, so He turned to him and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. Perhaps by His saying ﴿and loosen a knot from my tongue﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27] He alluded to what Allah bestowed upon him of facilitating this Remembrance through his tongue. And by the supplication of Moses (peace be upon him), for expansion of the breast, ease of affairs, and seeking a minister from his family, He guided to supplicating with the like of that, until the one upon whom this Qur'an was sent down supplicated that Allah strengthen the religion through one of the two men, and He strengthened it with the greatest minister: Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. This has passed, to the completion of what the context of the story of Moses (peace be upon him) includes here, completing the rebuke of the Jews for teaching the Quraysh to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Spirit, and what is mentioned along with it of subtleties from the matter of the story of their Prophet (ﷺ), which none of them knows, or only their most skilled, among them: that the appointment was on the Day of the Festival; among them the complete faith of the magicians; among them the threat of crucifying them on palm trunks; among them the Samiri's casting of the Messenger's trace. For I have not seen any of the Jews who knows that, and some of their learned men informed me that there is no mention of it among them.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said in his Burhan (Proof): When the Most High mentioned the story of Abraham (peace be upon him) and what He granted and bestowed upon him, and the stories of the Prophets after him with what He specified them with (p-274), and followed that with His saying: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favour from among the prophets, of the offspring of Adam﴾ [Maryam: 58], the apparent sense of the speech was the specification of these people with these lofty ranks and exalted, sublime degrees, especially since He followed it with His saying: ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and followed desires, so they will meet error﴾ [Maryam: 59]. This was a cause for apprehension and fear. So the Most High followed it with gentle address to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), the gentle address of the beloved, the drawn-near, the chosen, and said: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2]. Also, Surat Maryam was concluded with His saying: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them? Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them any sound?﴾ [Maryam: 98], after His saying: ﴿and you warn thereby a people contentious﴾ [Maryam: 97]. And upon him be prayer and peace, he saw from the Quraysh's delay in accepting Islam and their obstinacy what necessitated his apprehension and fear for them. There is no doubt that upon him be prayer and peace, the delay in their faith grieved him, and for this reason it was said to him: "Do not grieve over them." It was as if he (upon him be prayer and peace) thought that the desired goal of their response was difficult, or that hope of their repentance would be cut off, so the toil and hardship would be prolonged. So the Most High gave him good news by His saying: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2]. So do not concern yourself with the obstinacy and hesitation of these people; whoever harbours fear will respond when reminded and stirred to contemplate the signs of Allah, as it was said to him in another place: ﴿So let not their statement grieve you﴾ [Ya-Sin: 76]. Then the Most High followed that, by way of introduction and reassurance, with His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], up to the beginning of the stories of Moses (peace be upon him). So He informed that all is His creation and His dominion, under His subjugation and grip, and nothing deviates from His dominion (p-275). Whoever witnesses the sign of the One Who grants success to him, his affair will not be difficult. Then He followed that with the story of Moses (peace be upon him), and what occurred from him in casting him as a child into the river, and what happened after that of wondrous craftsmanship, the destruction of Pharaoh, and the emergence of the Children of Israel. All of this confirms the previously stated purpose. And this second aspect is preferable to the first, and Allah knows best. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 10:

﴿Idh﴾ (when): i.e., the account of him, when ﴿he saw a fire﴾ while he was returning from the lands of Madyan. ﴿So he said to his family, "Stay here"﴾: i.e., remain where you are and leave off the journey you were on. Then he gave a reason for his command with his words: ﴿"Indeed, I have perceived a fire"﴾: i.e., I have seen clearly, in this darkness, a sight free of doubt, by the pupil of the eye through which things are made manifest. And it is, along with that, something that gives delight from the people of companionship, who are present, [though] he had left no fire among them. So it is as if it were said: "And what then?" He said, expressing it with the particle of hope (la'alla), in order to restrict the report, which he expressed in an-Naml with "guidance": ﴿"Perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand"﴾: i.e., I hope to bring you to you, ﴿a burning brand﴾, meaning a flame of fire at the head of a piece of firewood that has an ember in it, which helps against the cold of this night; ﴿or I will find at the fire﴾, i.e., at the place of the fire, ﴿guidance﴾: i.e., something by which I may be guided, because the road had become hidden from them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 11:

﴿Then when he came to it﴾.

Since there was, in the indefiniteness followed by the specification, an arousing of eagerness and then of magnification, he built the verb in the passive voice, saying: ﴿he was called﴾, from the Guide who has no guide other than Him. Then he specified the calling by his saying (p-276): ﴿O Moses﴾. Since the situation called for introducing him through the bounties bestowed upon him, out of gentleness, he said it emphatically, as an alert [to him] to recognize that it is the speech of Him, glorified is He, coming from a direction in that He makes him hear it without any specific direction, and in a manner other than the form he was accustomed to in conversation with created beings. He dropped the particle (of address) in the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Hafs, who read it with a fatha, and he related it by means of an implied saying according to the rest of the readers:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, I am your Lord⦆ i.e., the One who bestows favour upon you by creation, provision, and other benefits of both abodes. ﴿So take off your sandals⦆ as is done in the presence of kings, out of courtesy, and so that its blessing may reach you, and so that you may be prepared for residence, not turning towards what lies behind you of family and children. For this reason, the people of expression (ahl al-'ibarah, the interpreters of dreams) said: "The sandal indicates a child."

Then he gave a reason that points to the fact that He, may He be exalted, is not contained by a place nor does time pass over Him, so he said: ﴿Indeed, you are in the sacred valley⦆ i.e., the purified one, cleansed of everything unfitting for the courtyards of kings; then he explained it by his saying: ﴿Tuwa⦆. Since the meaning is: "I have chosen it, honouring it above the [other] spots for your intimate conversation," he joined to it his saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 13:

﴿And I have chosen you﴾, that is, for prophethood. ﴿So listen﴾, that is, be attentive, casting your hearing and inclining your heart to listening. ﴿To what﴾, that is, I have chosen you for that which ﴿is revealed﴾, that is, it is said to you by Me in secret, hidden from others [its hearing], even though it is in the utmost openness, as the beloved does with his beloved by guarding their conversation from a third party, by granting them seclusion as a notification of the elevation of his rank and the magnificence of his affair.

Then he explained the revelation with the first of the obligations, which is knowledge of God, exalted is He. So He said, [emphasizing the greatness of the news and its departure from customary matters]: ﴿Indeed, I am God﴾. He mentioned the proper name (ism 'alam) because this is its proper station, since what suits the one who has been shown kindness (al-maltuf bihi), after being made acquainted with Him through honor, is to dwell in the station of majesty and beauty.

Since this proper name comprises all the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names (al-asma' al-husna, the divine names), which are too exalted for anyone other than God, Most High, to be truly described by them or by any of them, it was fitting that it be followed by His saying: ﴿There is no god but I﴾. And since the obligation to single Him out in worship follows from this, He said: ﴿So worship Me﴾, meaning, Me alone. Then He singled out from among the acts of worship the place of intimacy and solitude, the sign of humility and watchfulness, and the spirit of religion, and said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning the prayer that the successors of evil (khulűf al-su') had neglected, indicating that it is the primary purpose of religion, because it is the highest of its legislated acts, since it leads to watchfulness through its continual remembrance and its turning away from every evil. This is the meaning of ﴿for My remembrance﴾. This is the most fitting of all things for the station of majesty; indeed, it combines both manifestations of beauty and majesty.

Then He gave the reason for the command to worship, namely that He did not create creation in vain (sudan), but it is necessary that they be made to die and then be resurrected, to manifest His greatness and set up the scales of justice. So He said [emphasizing against their denial, and expressing it in a way that indicates how very easy that is for Him -]: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾, meaning there is no doubt about its coming, and so it is the greatest incentive to obedience.

(p-278) Since clarifying the reality of a thing while concealing its specific identity, its time, and all its circumstances usually leads to forgetting it and turning away from it, and since it was not far from concealing it altogether and entirely, He said, pointing to this meaning: ﴿I am almost concealing it﴾ [meaning: I am close to renewing its concealment. Therefore the disbeliever denies it with his tongue, and the disobedient denies it through his disobedience. The disbeliever does not affirm that it will happen, and the believer does not prepare himself, out of heedlessness of it -], so keep watch over Me, for the matter will come suddenly; there is not a moment but it is suitable for expectation. Then he explained the reason for its coming by His saying: ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed﴾, meaning with the easiest and most effective matter, ﴿for what it strives﴾ — meaning, what it produces through striving at every time, just as one who orders people to do a work does by examining their deeds and recompensing each according to what it deserves.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 16:

Since (what was mentioned earlier) placed him, in the judgment of most people, in the category of one who is forgotten, He said: ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾, that is, from continually remembering it, so that this would bear fruit in exerting oneself to prepare for it, ﴿from one who does not believe in it﴾ by his turning away from it and his burdening others to do the same by adorning for them what he has been given of worldly goods, which causes excessive accumulation, which in turn fills the heart with boasting and vainglory. For whoever is turned away from that is not far in condition from one who has denied it. (p-279) The intended meaning of the expression is the prohibition of Musa (peace be upon him) from denial, but it was expressed as the prohibition of one who does not believe from turning (him) away, out of honor for Musa (peace be upon him). Also, the turning away of the disbelievER from belief is a cause of denial, so He mentioned the cause to indicate the effect. Also, the turning away of the disbeliever results from the laxity of the man in religion and the softness of his resolve, so He mentioned the effect to indicate the cause. It is as if it were said: Be firm of resolve and steadfast of disposition, so that no one will hope to turn you away, even if those who turn away are a vast multitude, for their multitude reaches (only) to desire, not to proof. In this there is a great exhortation to act upon evidence, a powerful deterrent from blind imitation (taqlid), and a warning that destruction and perdition come with taqlid and its adherents; this was pointed out by al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf. Then he explained the reason for denying it and for slackness in striving for it, with His saying: ﴿and follows his desire﴾, that is, with the utmost of his effort, ﴿his desire﴾, so his state became the state of the beasts that have no intellect, as a warning against a state like his; then he magnified the warning with His saying, as a consequence: ﴿lest you perish﴾, that is, lest you be destroyed, indicating that whoever abandons vigilance for a moment swerves from the proof, and whoever swerves from the proof perishes.

When the situation called for the question, "What is your answer, O Musa, to what you have heard?", and He, exalted is He, knew that he would hasten to answer with obedience in everything that had preceded, He left this statement unspoken, alluding to it by joining to it His saying: ﴿And what is that﴾, meaning the high-valued one [p-280] ﴿in your right hand, O Musa?﴾. After putting him at ease by asking him about what He knows better than he does, He intended to establish proof before him, through something that would serve as evidence of the immediacy of power in bringing into existence what did not exist: turning the staff into a serpent. This would come after he had confirmed that it was a staff, by looking at it closely when he was asked about it, so that he would thereby gain greater firmness and strengthen those to whom he would be sent.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 20, verse 18:**

﴿He said: "It is my staff"﴾, that is, outwardly and inwardly. Then he joined to it, enjoying the sweetness of addressing (Allah), his words explaining its benefits, out of fear of being commanded to throw it down like a sandal:

﴿"I lean on it"﴾, that is, I rely on it, lean on it, and steady myself with it, ﴿"upon it"﴾, that is, when I am exhausted, or when something arises that requires me to do so, such as slipping, descending, ascending, leaping, darkness, or the like. Then, after the benefit to himself, he added the matter of his flock, saying:

﴿"And I beat down (with it the leaves) for my sheep"﴾. That is, I strike the leaves. Ibn Kathir said: Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim related from Imam Malik: "The hashsh (هَشّ) is that one places the crook (al-mihjan, a hooked staff) on the branch and then shakes it until its leaves and fruit fall, without breaking the stick or beating it. This is the hashsh." He said: Maymun ibn Mihran also said likewise. Abu Hayyan said: The root meaning of this word (هَشّ) is softness (al-rakhāwa). It is said: "a man is hashsh" (رَجُلٌ هَشٌّ), meaning soft and gentle.

﴿"with it, upon my sheep"﴾.

Since he was the most perfect of the people of that time, he feared prolonging the conversation before the King, so he cut short for himself what he was enjoying of the sweetness of addressing (Allah), as it is said: "Sit upon the carpet, and beware of overfamiliarity." Yet out of eagerness to hear the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, he spoke in a summary manner: ﴿"And I have in it other uses"﴾, that is, needs and benefits which the intelligent will understand. [Since the one spoken of is inanimate, and he referred to it with a plural of multitude, the more appropriate treatment was to treat it as a feminine singular, so he said —]: ﴿"other uses"﴾, leaving the details aside. It is as if it was said: "What was he then told?" So it was said:

Translation:

﴿He said, "Throw it down"﴾, that is, the staff. He put him at ease by His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿O Musa﴾.

﴿So he threw it﴾, that is, as a consequence of this command that was obeyed, he threw it and did not hesitate. ﴿And behold, it was﴾, that is, immediately, outwardly and inwardly, ﴿a serpent﴾, very great, which because of its size and the extreme state of its condition is called by the name *tho'ban* (thu'bān, a large serpent), while *ḥayyah* (serpent) is a generic noun that applies to the male and the female, the young and the old. ﴿Moving swiftly﴾, a light, quick motion, for which it was called at the beginning of its condition *jann* (jann, a snake that moves quickly). Thus Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, reported that it became a yellow serpent with a mane like the mane of a horse, and it began to swell until it became a *thuʿbān*, – end of quote. So it was in the size of a *thuʿbān* and the swiftness of a *jann*.

Since that was a frightening matter, the listener was eager to know what would become of him in such a situation afterward, so He resumed informing him with His saying: ﴿He said﴾, that is, God, blessed and exalted is He, speaking of what would happen to it before Pharaoh, for the sake of training: (p-282) ﴿Take it and do not fear﴾, indicating that he had feared it according to the custom of human nature. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition against fear with His saying ﴿We shall return it﴾, that is, by Our might, when you take it, with a promise that will not fail, ﴿to its former state﴾, that is, its manner, ﴿the first﴾, from being a staff. So this is a clear sign that the One who addresses you is your Lord, to whom belong the Most Beautiful Names. Thus tranquility descended upon him, and his confidence reached the point that he put his hand into its mouth and seized it by its beard, and behold, it was his staff again, and his hand between its two forks.

[And when He showed him one sign in one of the horizons, He wished to show him a sign within himself, so He said -]: ﴿And draw your hand﴾ into your collar, through which your neck emerges, ﴿to your wing﴾, i.e., to your side beneath the upper arm, and it will be drawn in, returning to what it was in its color and without the burning that was in it. And take it out, and it will come out. So the verse is of the type of ihtibak (the figure of omission in which each of two complementary elements is left implicit where the other is stated). The "janah" (wing) means: the hand, the upper arm, the armpit, and the side, as stated in al-Qamus (the lexicon). Therefore, this does not contradict what is in Surah al-Qasas, because there He used "janah" for the hand, which is more deserving of the term, while here it refers to the side, which is its place, by naming the location after what is located in it (metonymy). ﴿white﴾ with a whiteness like the sun, at which one marvels.

And since leprosy was the most hated thing to the Arabs, He said, negating it and anything else, and did not name it explicitly, because their ears recoil from it, and because negating the general category of a thing is more eloquent than negating it specifically: ﴿without harm﴾, i.e., without illness, neither leprosy nor anything else, ﴿as another sign﴾, do what I have commanded you of casting the staff and drawing in the hand, or We did that as a transformation of the staff and the color of the hand, from Our calling you to Our intimate conversation.

"So that We may show you" (﴿لِنُرِيَكَ﴾) during all the days of your prophethood "of Our greatest signs" (﴿مِن آياتِنا الكُبْرى﴾), so that your heart may thereby be made firm (لِيَثْبُتَ بِذَلِكَ جَنانُكَ) and your mastery (إتْقانُكَ) may increase. It is as if it were said: "Why does He do this with me?" And it was said: "So that We may send you on some important missions."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 24:

﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾, that is, so that you may turn him back from his arrogant transgression. Then he gave the reason for sending him to Pharaoh with his words, [emphasizing that the transgression of anyone, in relation to anything belonging to the Most High King, is something to be deemed far-fetched -]: ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾, that is, he went beyond his limit of servanthood and claimed lordship. He indicated what befell him of distress because of this by what he knew of it, that it is a great matter and a grave affair, which requires with it the enduring of what none can endure except one with a steadfast heart, a broad breast [and a controlled spirit -] as he stated in [Surat ash-Shu'ara'] with his words

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 25:

﴿He said: "My Lord, expand for me"﴾ i.e., widen (for me). Since he left the thing to be expanded unspecified, so that the speech would be more emphatic through repeating the meaning in the two modes of generality (ijmal) and detail (tafsil), he said, specifying that unspecified matter: ﴿my breast﴾, for undertaking that, and for finding it difficult, by his saying:

﴿And make easy for me﴾ [then he clarified that ambiguity with his saying -]: ﴿my task﴾ [and [it points] to his deeming himself incapable of making clear to them the intended meaning, by his saying -]:

(p-284) ﴿And loosen﴾. Since the meaning here is one that admits of no other (for he did not ask that it remain in any state other than that of the call), he turned away from the pattern of the preceding speech and said: ﴿a knot from my tongue﴾, that is, of the impediment that is in it, preventing him from conveying all the intended meanings, arising from the live coal which he (Pharaoh) placed in his mouth while he was in the presence of Pharaoh, as has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father,

Since his request was made purely for the sake of God, he limited himself to what was necessary and did not ask for the removal of his whole impediment. Therefore He answered him with His words: ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾. And [his request for] support, through a helper who would take his affair to heart, was [made] with the belief that the task was difficult despite all of this, [and he said]:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 29:

﴿And appoint for me﴾ i.e., [from among what –] You bestow upon me; and he showed his concern for assistance as the situation demands, so he put forward his saying: ﴿a minister﴾, i.e., a refuge who will bear some of the burden from me and help me, ﴿from my family﴾, because I am more trusting in him, for he is more compassionate toward me,

Then he substituted for it his saying: ﴿Harun﴾, and clarified it with his saying: ﴿my brother﴾ [i.e.,] because he was the most fitting of my family for the complete support of me. And he answered the supplication in the recitation of Ibn 'Amir, so he said:

Surah 20, verse 31:

﴿Strengthen﴾ [with the hamza cut and vowelled with a fatha] ﴿my back through him﴾, that is, my strength and my back.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 32:

﴿And make him a partner﴾ — read with a dammah on the hamza, the two verbs being attributed to his (Moses') pronoun, on the basis that they are both imperfect verbs (muḍāriʿ). The reading of the rest of the readers is with a connecting alif on the first and a fathah on the hamza of the second, on the basis that they are both imperatives (amr), attributed to God the Exalted in the form of a supplication, ﴿in my affair﴾, i.e., the prophethood.

When his request made clear that he had purposes in it, he indicated that these were not his ultimate aim for a matter that returns to himself, by mentioning the true cause, so he said: ﴿That we may glorify You greatly﴾, i.e., by word and deed, through prayer and other acts, ﴿greatly﴾. Thus he made clear that the purpose of seeking support was only to pave the way to Him, glorified is He.

Since tasbih (glorifying God by affirming His transcendence, the highest form of which is tawhid) is a specific kind of remembrance, he followed it with the general kind, saying: ﴿And that we may remember You﴾ — that is, with glorification and praise — ﴿abundantly﴾. For mutual cooperation and support aid in the increase of worship, because it stirs up the desires.

Then he gave a reason for his request for his brother, for this purpose, by saying: ﴿Indeed You have always been Seeing of us﴾ before the establishment of this matter, in that You fashioned us in a way that suits Your remembrance and Your gratitude, and that mutual support is something that sets us right; and all of this is a training for the one upon whom this Reminder was sent down, for the like of it, and a reminder of the blessing of its being made easy by his tongue, so that he may increase in remembrance and gratitude.

Now that this had been completed, it was the place where a response was anticipated, so He followed it with His saying: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Allah: ﴿You have been given﴾ with the easiest of matters ﴿your request﴾, that is, what you asked Him for ﴿O Moses﴾, regarding the loosening of the knot of your tongue and other than that. Had I wished, I would not have done that; but I did it as a favor from Me to you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 37:

Since his deliverance from Pharaoh, in that he was born in the year in which Pharaoh was slaughtering the sons (they said: this was the fourth year after the birth of Harun, peace be upon him), by the hand of Pharaoh and in his house, was a great matter, he turned to the station of majesty (maqam al-'azamah), reminding him of that in order to illuminate his insight (tanwiran li-basiratihi) and strengthen his heart (taqwiyatan li-qalbihi), informing him that He would deliver him from him now, just as He delivered him in that time, and would increase him in goodness with the increase of his age and prophethood, so that He would make his might lie in his destruction, just as He made his might at that time lie in his existence. So He said: ﴿And We had already bestowed upon you⁠﴾, that is, We conferred a bounty certain to be realized, befitting Our majesty, ﴿upon you⁠﴾ as a favor from Us, ﴿another time⁠﴾ other than this one;

Then he mentioned the time of the favor, saying: ﴿When﴾, that is, at the time when ﴿We revealed﴾ [that is, by what We possess of greatness -] ﴿to your mother﴾, that is, by inspiration, "that which" is worthy, given His greatness, to be "revealed" with it, and which none knows except a prophet or one who is close to the rank of prophethood;

Then he explained it with His words: ﴿Cast him into the chest﴾, that is, cast your son ﴿into the chest﴾, which is the box (ṣundūq). It is on the pattern fa'ūl from *al-tawb*, whose meaning is "return," optimistically (tafā'ulan) by it. Al-Harrālī said: it is a container for what is precious. The word *qadhf* (casting) is used figuratively for hastening to place him without any delay at all, indicating that the act is guaranteed safety in whatever way it is done. The definite article is used because it is a type of box that the people most familiar with it are the Children of Israel. ﴿Then cast him﴾, that is, [Mūsā, peace be upon him,] immediately after that, with his chest, or the chest in which Mūsā, peace be upon him, was, ﴿into the sea (yamm)﴾, that is, the river, which is the Nile.

Since his safety in the sea was one of the wonders, because he was exposed to drowning through the wind overturning the chest, or its breaking against some walls or other things, or its flowing straight with the strongest current of the water into the salt sea, and other calamities, He indicated the certainty of his deliverance with the imperative particle *lām*, expressing the meaning of a report in His words, making the sea as if it were discerning so that it would obey the command: ﴿So let the sea cast him onto the bank﴾, that is, the chest in which Mūsā, peace be upon him, was, or Mūsā with his chest, ﴿the sea onto the shore﴾, that is, the bank of the Nile. It was named *sāḥil* because the water drags it (yasḥaluhu), that is, spreads it, to the side of the house. The whole act is for fleeing from the evil of its owner, who is Pharaoh, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿will take him﴾, as an answer to the command, that is, Mūsā, ﴿an enemy to Me﴾. He drew attention to the point of wonder by repeating the word "enemy" in His words: ﴿and an enemy to him﴾, for he did not oppose the Children of Israel by slaughtering them except for his sake. ﴿And I cast upon you love﴾, that is, great love. Then He increased the explanation of its greatness with His words: ﴿from Me﴾, [that is,] so that everyone who sees you will love you, because of the good qualities and sound characteristics with which I have endowed you, so that you would be fit for what I intend you for. ﴿And that you may be raised﴾, that is, reared in the easiest manner of upbringing by one who is constantly with you and never ceases to take great care of your interests ﴿under My eye﴾, that is, standing above your guardians, not hidden from anyone in your upbringing, nor feared for you from him, and I am a guardian for you, the guarding of one who watches a thing with his eye and never lets it out of sight. So everything I wished came to pass. When this enemy saw you, he loved you and sought wet-nurses for you; when you did not accept any of them, he pressed the search further. All of this was the carrying out of My command and the restraining of his command by himself, not by anyone else, so that the wonder at the precision of the cause would increase.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 40:

Then he mentioned the time of the (divine) crafting, saying: ﴿When﴾, i.e., at the time when ﴿your sister walked﴾, i.e., in the place where they had put you, to find for you a nursing woman. ﴿She said﴾, after she had seen you, to the household of Pharaoh: ﴿Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?﴾, i.e., who will look after his needs of nursing and service, sincerely caring for him. They said: "Yes!" So she brought your mother, and you took her breast. ﴿So We returned you﴾, i.e., as a consequence of her words, We returned you ﴿to your mother﴾ when they were directed to her, ﴿that her eye might be cooled﴾, i.e., might become cool and calm, and that she might raise you, secure about you, not fearful, openly and not in hiding. ﴿And that she would not grieve﴾ over your separation or over the lack of her raising [of you -] and her exertion of effort for your benefit. ﴿And you killed a soul﴾, i.e., after you had become a man, from among the Copts, in defense of a man from your people, for which you were sought and they intended to kill you. ﴿So We delivered you﴾ by what We possess of greatness ﴿from distress﴾ that had befallen you on account of killing him, from fear of the consequence of his blood, by bringing you out as a migrant from their lands toward Madyan. ﴿And We tried you with a trying﴾, i.e., We rescued you from one ordeal after another, time after time, (p-289) whether it is the plural of fitn or fitnah (with the ta' not counted), or it may be a verbal noun like shakur. So the ordeals were: your birth in the year of the slaughter, your being left in the river, then your being denied suckling from anyone's breast other than your mother's, then your pulling at Pharaoh's beard, then your taking the ember instead of the dinar, then your killing of the Copt, then your departure toward Madyan on the dangerous road, fearful and watchful, then your hiring yourself out for ten years, then your losing the way, then the scattering of your flock on a dark night. ﴿Then you stayed years﴾, i.e., many, ﴿among the people of Madyan﴾, residing with our prophet Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, who raised you with his manners, and you were united with him through his daughter. ﴿Then you came﴾, i.e., now, ﴿at an appointed time﴾, i.e., a time that I had decreed from eternity for My speaking to you, which is the attainment of full maturity and maturity of strength, and for sending you to Pharaoh so that I might carry out through you My decree that he had slaughtered the sons of the Children of Israel out of fear of him. So you came neither ahead of time nor behind it. ﴿O Musa!﴾

Translation:

﴿And I have chosen you﴾, i.e., I raised you with the works of kindness, the upbringing of one who takes pains to form the one he rears in a certain manner, ﴿for Myself﴾, i.e., so that you would do, in pleasing Me by laying the foundations of My laws and carrying out My commands, what is done by one who is fashioned for himself without any partner. It is thus an image of the station of nearness and honour that surrounds it.

So when all of that had been laid out, after the knowledge of its outcome, He repeated it in His saying: ﴿Go, you and your brother﴾, as I previously commanded you, ﴿with My signs﴾ which I showed you (p-290) and others that I manifest through your hands, ﴿and do not slacken﴾, that is, do not become languid or weak, ﴿in remembering Me﴾, which was previously mentioned that you made the goal of your supplication. Rather, let it be - while it is an all-encompassing frame for your entire affair - in the utmost striving within it and in bringing the heart to it. And let it be most of all at the meeting with Pharaoh, for surely My servant, [My] servant entirely, is the one who remembers Me at the meeting with his adversary, for that is the greatest help toward the goal.

Then he specified the destination by His saying, emphasizing the going itself, because given the great danger, human nature hardly comes to firmly believe in the command to go: ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh﴾. Then he gave the reason for sending them to him by His saying, emphasizing what preceded it, and to increase the wonder at his lack of intellect, so how about those who followed him: ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾.

Then He commanded them with what befits everyone who enjoins the good, namely taking the most gentle course first, then the next most gentle, then the easiest after that. So He said, as a consequence of arriving at this point and as a sequel to it: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear.﴾ [This is so that he leaves no argument for himself and accepts no excuse,] ﴿perhaps he will remember﴾ what has passed for him of God's shaping of him through different stages, and of His carrying him, in matters he dislikes, to a point where he could not escape by any stratagem. Thereby he will know that God is his Lord and that He is able to do what He wills with him, so he will turn back from his error and believe. ﴿Or fear﴾, that is, or he will reach the state of one who fears the consequence of your words, since he supposes them to be true, [so your words will be a reminder to him], and then he will send the Children of Israel with you.

The meaning of "perhaps" (al-tarajji) is that his state should be like that of one from whom such a thing is hoped for, because it is among the fruits of gentleness in calling. The discourse in this and similar places follows what people customarily understand in their conversations, and the Qur'an came in their language and according to what they mean. Thus the intended sense is: "Go, you two, upon your hope, your expectation, and the extent of your knowledge; you have no more than this, since you do not know [the outcome]. As for His knowledge, may He be exalted, it comes from behind what will occur." This is what Sibawayh said in the chapter on the indefinite noun that functions like what contains the alif and lam of verbal nouns and nouns.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 45:

When Pharaoh was at the utmost of tyranny, and his condition was that of one who would kill them both unless Allah prevented him, and [Moses and Aaron] wished to know what would happen as a result of that, ﴿They said: "Our Lord"﴾, that is, "O You who are benevolent to us." Since the substance of their report [of fear together with] their being from Allah's side is something whose nature is not to be (i.e., it is not to be expected) and to be denied, they emphasised it, saying it with great emphasis by making the third nūn (of the verb) clearly pronounced, in order to make the complaint fully manifest, so that the consolation would come in proportion to the brokenness that appears: ﴿Indeed we fear﴾ because of what he possesses of power, ﴿that he will hasten﴾, that is, act hastily, ﴿against us﴾ with punishment before the delivery of the message is complete, with the haste of one who springs upon and leaps at a thing, ﴿or that he will transgress﴾, so that he exceeds to something greater than what he is in of arrogance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 46:

﴿He said: "Do not fear."﴾ Then He gave the reason for this with that which is the basis of support and protection for the one who is an ally, and of destruction for the enemy. So He said, emphasizing it to indicate the greatness of the news (p-292) and to draw attention to its content, because it is outside of customary practice, and He kept the third nun, in conformity with the pattern of their two emphatic forms: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both﴾, not absent as kings are absent when they send their messengers, ﴿Hearing and seeing﴾, that is, these two attributes are Mine; nothing of the condition of My messenger, nor of the condition of his enemy, is hidden from Me, and you both know of My power what no one else knows besides you two.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 47:

When this was firmly established, there followed from it the instruction to them as to what they should say. So He said, emphasizing the going (of the two) again, as before: ﴿So come to him and say﴾, that is, to him. And since Pharaoh denied what their statement contained, Glorified is He, He emphasized it, saying: ﴿Indeed, we﴾. And since the indication of the meaning of support (mu'azara) was here required, as was mentioned before, He repeated it, saying: ﴿are two messengers of your Lord﴾, the One who nurtured you and raised you well after He brought you into being from non-existence, as an indication of belittling him, that he is among the number of the servants of the One who sent the two of them, refuting him in his claim to lordship. Then He made the sending of you two to him the cause of your saying: ﴿So send with us﴾ His servants ﴿the Children of Israel﴾ so that they may worship Him, for none deserves worship but Him, ﴿and do not torment them﴾ with what you torment them with of enslavement and slaughter. Then He gave a reason for the claim of messengerhood with what establishes it, saying, opening with the particle of expectation, because the state of the hearer of a claim of messengerhood is to expect a sign indicating the sending: ﴿We have certainly brought you a sign﴾, that is, a great sign, proof and demonstration (p-293) ﴿from your Lord﴾, the One from whom alone any favor upon you comes, one that necessitates acceptance of what we have claimed, of the staff, the hand and other things. So submit, and you will be safe. In repeating the address to him with this, there is emphasis to rebuke him over his claim to lordship, and to ascribe to him ingratitude for favor. ﴿And peace is upon﴾ him specifically if you accept the guidance of God. ﴿And peace﴾, that is, its genus, ﴿upon﴾ all ﴿those who follow﴾ with the utmost of their effort ﴿the guidance﴾, in general. And when this genus of peace is upon them, it is known that ruin is upon others. So the meaning is: [and] if you refuse, you will be punished.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 48:

﴿Indeed we﴾, i.e., because we ﴿have been revealed to﴾ from our Lord ﴿that the punishment﴾, i.e., all of it, since the lam (in al-ʿadhāb, "the punishment") is either for comprehensiveness (lil-istighrāq) or for the reality of the category (lil-māhiyyah), and under either of the two interpretations it implies the degree of the establishment and permanence of this kind, owing to what the nominal sentence conveys, ﴿is upon﴾ every ﴿one who denies and turns away﴾, i.e., who commits denial and aversion. This implies that if any of it falls upon one who affirms the truth, it is temporary, and once it has ended it is as if it had never existed. Diverting the speech away from him (i.e., not directly addressing the one who is guided) serves as an indication that he is a misguided denier, and as a lesson in good manners (adab).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 20, verse 49:

Since the implied meaning was: "So come to him and say: Indeed we are the messengers of your Lord" – to the end of what they were commanded to say – and their statement contained that the one who sent them has complete power and all-encompassing knowledge, his question about identifying Him followed as a consequence. He resumed reporting his answer with the words: ﴿He said﴾, i.e., Pharaoh, repelling them by way of debate and not by way of force, so that he would not be attributed to (p-294) foolishness and ignorance: ﴿Who then﴾, i.e., as a consequence of this speech of yours, which none of the people of the earth dares to confront me with, is the one I should ask you about: who is ﴿your Lord﴾ who sent you? He did not say "my Lord," as a way of evading the straight line of reasoning and diverting the speech away from the manner that would make his disgrace clear.

Since Musa (peace be upon him) was the principal one in this matter, and since Pharaoh might have hoped, through his deceit and bad method, that there was some impediment (ḥubsah) occurring in his tongue, he singled him out with the words: ﴿O Musa﴾

Musa replied to him at once: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation﴾, that is, our Creator, Nurturer and Master, ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾ of all that you see in existence, ﴿then guided it﴾. He gave each thing what suits it, in terms of the benefits attached to it and the effects that proceed from it, such as its form, shape, measure, colour, nature and other things that cannot be counted and are beyond description.

Since the bestowing of the soul carries such majesty and greatness that everything else in comparison to it becomes insignificant in its differences, he indicated this with the particle of delay (thumma), saying: ﴿then guided﴾, that is, every living creature among them, although among them are the rational and others, to all its benefits so that it strives for them, and to its harms so that it avoids them. Through this variation and differentiation, while the relation of all things to the Agent is one, it is established that He is one and free in choice, and that if this were by nature, dependent upon the stars or other things, as Pharaoh and others believed, this variation would not exist.

Since no one could find fault with this answer before, because it has no slip or flaw, and because of its elegance, its brevity, and its precedence in gathering meanings to the end of its field, (Pharaoh) turned the speech quickly, fearing clarity and Moses (peace be upon him) increasing in explanation. Thus the corruption would appear from what is sound, and he moved to a matter with wide scope, on which no proof stands, so that refutation is possible in it. So Allah, glorified is He, reported about it in the mode of *istinaf* (resumed speech, a new sentence that answers an implied question), with His saying: ﴿He said, "Then what about the former generations?"﴾. That is, it follows from what this contained of ascribing to your Lord knowledge of every existing thing: "I say to you, what then is the state (*bal*) of the former generations?" That is, the report of the former generations, which is of such greatness that it did not mix with anyone without transforming him and turning him away -]. And although it was an evasion, it is one of the signs of being unable to answer, yet it is an act firmly rooted in deceit and trickery.

Then he pointed to a detailed account of the wisdom in it, with his words, as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "We brought forth" (akhrajnā): ﴿Eat﴾, that is, of what He has arranged for you in His wisdom from it, ﴿and graze﴾, that is, send out to the pastures, ﴿your livestock﴾, which He has made fit for them and which is not suitable for you.
